lesson.title: Divide and Conquer: The Merge Sort Strategy
lesson.summary: Merge sort tackles sorting with decomposition: it splits a list into smaller pieces, sorts the pieces, and then merges those sorted pieces back together using a simple, reliable merge step.
lesson.body:
Selection sort and insertion sort both work directly on the whole list, gradually growing a sorted section within it. Merge sort takes a different philosophy, one rooted in decomposition: break a hard problem into smaller pieces, solve each piece, and combine the solutions. This general strategy is often called divide and conquer, and merge sort is the classic example of it applied to sorting.

The plan has three parts. Divide the list into two halves. Conquer each half by sorting it (we will see in the next chapter that this "conquer" step is where recursion enters the picture). Combine the two sorted halves into a single sorted list. This chapter focuses on that last part, the combine step, usually called merge, since understanding how to merge two already-sorted lists is the key mechanical piece that makes the whole strategy work.

Merging two sorted lists is simpler than it might sound. Since both lists are already in order, the smallest element overall must be at the front of one of the two lists. So look at the front of each list, take whichever one is smaller, and add it to the result. Repeat until one list runs out, then append whatever remains of the other list, since everything left in it is already sorted and bigger than everything you have taken so far.

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

Trace merge(left, right) with left = [2, 7, 9] and right = [1, 4, 8, 10].

Compare left[0]=2 and right[0]=1. 1 is smaller, so take 1: result = [1], j moves to 1.
Compare left[0]=2 and right[1]=4. 2 is smaller, so take 2: result = [1, 2], i moves to 1.
Compare left[1]=7 and right[1]=4. 4 is smaller, so take 4: result = [1, 2, 4], j moves to 2.
Compare left[1]=7 and right[2]=8. 7 is smaller, so take 7: result = [1, 2, 4, 7], i moves to 2.
Compare left[2]=9 and right[2]=8. 8 is smaller, so take 8: result = [1, 2, 4, 7, 8], j moves to 3.
Compare left[2]=9 and right[3]=10. 9 is smaller, so take 9: result = [1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9], i moves to 3, which exhausts left.

Since left is now exhausted, the loop stops, and whatever remains of right, which is [10], is appended: result = [1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10]. That is exactly the sorted combination of the two input lists.

Each element from the two input lists is looked at exactly once during a merge, so merging two lists that together hold n elements takes O(n) time. The full merge sort algorithm applies this merge step over and over as it combines smaller sorted pieces into larger ones, and the next chapter looks at exactly how those smaller sorted pieces are produced in the first place, using recursion to repeatedly divide the list down to its simplest possible case.
